Hi Elaine / EdgePay team,

Thanks again for the demo earlier — good discussion. Per our call I wanted to capture the performance SLOs and proposed next steps so we have a clear runbook for qualification. Below is a concise recap plus the test plan attachments.

High-level targets (your ask + our suggested guardrails):
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): target p50 <= 120 ms, p95 <= 250 ms (we understand EdgePay is targeting p95 <= 300 ms; see notes for tradeoffs)
- Sustained throughput: ~350 requests/sec across the cluster (baseline traffic profile you shared)
- Concurrency: support for 800 concurrent active requests, with burst handling to ~1200 for short windows
- Streaming requirements: primary transport SSE (server-sent events); fallback WebSocket OK. Desired chunk cadence: 60-120 ms between frame boundaries at p95; chunk size typically 4-16 KB (depends on tokenization)
- Streaming semantics: progressive token flush per 1-2 tokens; we can configure chunk coalescing if your client prefers fewer, larger frames

Notes on measurement and sources of latency:
- TTFT measurement we use: time from our HTTP ingress receiving the request to the first model output byte sent (includes server-side TLS handshake for brand-new connections; excluded when keep-alive/connection pooling is used)
- Cold-starts (model load + kernel init) can add 200-600 ms depending on model/quantization and backing hardware; warm KV cache and pinned instances reduce TTFT significantly
- Network hops (client -> LB -> Redwood) and client-side parsing add outside our measurement; we recommend connection warm-up and keep-alives on your side for accurate SLO attainment

Recommended configuration to reliably meet TTFT targets:
1) Use persistent connections (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive for SSE or WebSocket) and connection pooling at your edge
2) Prefer Dedicated capacity or a pinned pool in Hosted to keep model instances warm during your peak windows
3) Enable prefix/KV caching for repeat prompts where applicable
4) If p95 TTFT is critical, configure a small pre-warm fleet and set autoscale thresholds to avoid reactive cold starts during scheduled windows

Attachments included: benchmark plan (redwood-benchmark-plan-v1.pdf) and a small sample of TTFT logs/format (redwood-ttft-data-sample.csv).

Next steps / asks for EdgePay:
- Confirm a testing window (we proposed a 30–60 minute controlled load window) and the staging endpoint + service account we should use
- IP allowlist / firewall rules we need for test agents (we'll provide IP ranges)
- Grant readonly access to your staging telemetry (or share sample traces) so we can align metrics

Proposed test: Redwood runs a 30-minute synthetic run that mirrors your token distribution and chunk cadence; we return a p50/p95 breakdown for TTFT, chunk cadence percentiles, and token-level throughput. If results show need for tuning, Vivek (cc'd) will propose concrete infra changes (cache pinning, instance sizing, kernel flags).

Availability for a follow-up call: Vivek and I are available 3/15–3/17 for a 30-min review.

Thanks — will start prepping the benchmark once you confirm staging details.

Best,
Marissa

Hi Elaine — quick technical note to address the questions Marissa captured. I'm listing explicit measurement definitions and pragmatic recommendations so the test run has deterministic expectations.

Measurement definitions (what Redwood will report):
- TTFT (server-side): timestamp at ingress (after TLS termination) -> timestamp of first byte written from the model-serving process. For dedicated/pinned instances TLS handshake time is effectively amortized (keep-alive) and excluded; for brand-new TCP/TLS handshakes it is included and recorded separately as "connection_setup_ms" in our report.
- Chunk cadence: measured as inter-arrival time between flush events on the response stream (ms). We report p50/p90/p95/p99 for cadence and per-chunk payload sizes (bytes).

SSE vs WebSocket: implementation notes
- SSE: standard text/event-stream is fine. Redwood will emit newline-terminated events and recommend using small flushes (1–4 tokens per event) if you need token-granular UI updates.
- WebSocket: provides lower overhead for high-frequency small frames; if you see jitter at the 60–120 ms cadence we can test both transports and report differences.

Cold-start mitigation and configuration knobs
- Pin a small pool of warm instances during the test window (reduces variance in TTFT).
- Preload common prompt prefixes into KV cache where applicable; this reduces model compute time for repeated beginnings of prompts.
- If using quantized models, prefer q4 or int8 profiles we've validated; some quantization paths have slightly higher initial kernel selection that affects first-token latency by ~20–50ms.

Suggested test parameters (what we'll run unless you ask to change):
- Duration: 30 minutes (steady-phase) with 5-minute ramp up/down
- Target concurrency: 600 active requests (matches your peak shapes)
- Request mix: 60% short prompts (<=128 tokens), 40% long prompts (300–700 tokens)
- Desired chunk cadence: 60ms nominal, measuring distribution across p50/p95/p99
- Instrumentation: we will push a results bundle (CSV + JSON summary) and a Grafana snapshot link to the drive folder we shared

Operational asks from EdgePay for the run:
- Staging endpoint + service account key (read-only is fine for telemetry)
- Allowlist the following Redwood agent IPs: 34.82.120.15, 34.82.120.16
- Confirm whether your ingress performs TLS termination or if we should expect end-to-end TLS through to our agent

If you confirm the window (Marissa has availability on 3/15 as well), I will own the benchmark execution and deliver the TTFT/cadence report with actionable tuning items.

Cheers,
Vivek Kulkarni
Senior Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
